summary: This memo describes how to carry DTMF signals, other tones and telephony events in RTP packets. It replaces RFC 2833, keeping only basic event codes and creating an IANA registry for more. It makes DTMF support optional, with implementations indicating supported events, and adds segmenting, multiple events per packet and state events.

eli5.summary: Phone keypad beeps can be sent as little notes instead of as sound. This explains how to write them into internet packets so the right button press arrives.

questions: how are dtmf digits sent over rtp
subtitle: How to carry keypad digits, ringing and busy signals, and other telephony events inside RTP packets instead of as fragile audio.

tldr.problem: Low-rate voice codecs cannot be trusted to reproduce touch tones accurately enough for machines to recognize them, and some telephone signals, such as on-hook, are not sounds at all.
tldr.mechanism: Two RTP payload formats: telephone-event, which names an event with a one-byte code and sends repeated updates of its running duration, and tone, which describes a tone by its frequencies, modulation and duration.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4733 replaces RFC 2833, keeps only the DTMF event codes and creates an IANA registry for others. It also adds long-event segments, several events per packet and state events, and requires message integrity.

today: RFC 4733 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2833. It has been updated by RFC 4734 and RFC 5244, and it has not itself been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Signals Need Their Own Payload
sections.content:
RFC 4733 defines two RTP payload formats. One carries dual-tone multifrequency (DTMF) digits and other line and trunk signals as named events. The other describes general multifrequency tones only by their frequency and cadence.

Separate formats exist because low-rate voice codecs cannot be guaranteed to reproduce tone signals accurately enough for automatic recognition, and properties such as the phase reversals in the ANSam tone do not survive speech coding. Separate formats also allow higher redundancy at a low bit rate, and some events, such as on-hook, occur out of band and cannot be sent as tones at all.

The RFC lists three ways to carry tone signals: switch to a higher-bandwidth codec such as G.711, send the measured frequencies with the tone format, or recognize the signal and send a code for it with the telephone-event format. Only the third works for out-of-band PSTN signals. Where exact timing against the audio is not important and data is unicast, a reliable control protocol may be preferable and this payload would not be used.
sections.eli5: A squeaky phone line can smear a beep so the other side cannot tell which button you pressed. So instead of sending the sound, the phone sends a note saying which button it was.

sections.title: The Telephone-Event Payload
sections.content:
The payload is named telephone-event (media type audio/telephone-event). It has no static payload type number; one is assigned dynamically and out of band, and the default clock rate is 8000 Hz. Events travel in the audio stream and MUST use the same sequence number and timestamp base as the regular audio, so the payload is treated like a very highly compressed audio codec.

The payload has four parts. The event field is a number from 0 to 255 naming the event. The E bit marks the end of the event. The R bit is reserved: senders MUST set it to zero and receivers MUST ignore it. The volume field gives the power level in dBm0 with the sign dropped, from 0 to -63, so larger values mean quieter. It is defined only for events whose documentation says volume applies; otherwise the sender MUST set it to zero. The duration field counts timestamp units since the event began, and at 8000 Hz it covers up to about 8 seconds.

In the RTP header, the timestamp marks the start of the event, so many packets for one event share a timestamp. The marker bit flags the start of a new event. A duration of zero is reserved for state events that last until updated, and senders MUST NOT send it for any other event.
sections.eli5: Each note says which button, whether it is finished, how loud, and how long it has been going. Every new note for the same press just updates the length.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Events
sections.content:
Capabilities are negotiated out of band, for example with SDP. A sender SHOULD list the events it supports in the optional events parameter, and when it receives such a list it MUST send only those events. If no list arrives it SHOULD assume only DTMF events 0 to 15. A receiver describing the payload in SDP MUST list the events it can process. The rate parameter gives the sampling rate and defaults to 8000 Hz.

A source SHOULD begin sending as soon as it recognizes an event and keep sending updates with the same timestamp and a growing cumulative duration. An update every 50 ms is RECOMMENDED. The first packet MUST have the M bit set and the final packet MUST have the E bit set, while intermediate packets MUST NOT have either. The final packet for each event or segment SHOULD be sent three times in total, optionally using RFC 2198 redundancy, so the end is recognized even if one copy is lost. The sequence number increases with every packet, including retransmissions.

An event that exceeds the largest duration (0xFFFF) is split into segments. The sender reports the maximum duration without the E bit, then starts a new segment whose timestamp is where the previous one ended and whose M bit is not set. Several events may share one packet only if they are consecutive and contiguous. The receiver can reconstruct a long event by checking that the new timestamp equals the previous timestamp plus 0xFFFF.

For playout, a receiver may place the tone in its buffer at the timestamp, or start the tone and play until the E bit, the next tone, other media, or a time limit. Either way the tone SHOULD NOT be extended by more than three packet interarrival times. A gateway is RECOMMENDED to render only the telephone-event payload when audio for the same instant also arrives, since the audio may contain spurious tones. If a soft state's duration expires, the receiver SHOULD treat its value as unknown.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps sending longer and longer updates while you hold the button, then repeats the final note three times in case one gets lost. The receiver plays the beep for as long as the notes say.

sections.title: Reliability and Congestion
sections.content:
Networks go through periods of congestion lasting on the order of a second, with higher delay, jitter and loss. The RFC lists impairments an implementation tries to limit: an event never played, a delayed start, a wrong duration, gaps in playout, and excessive end-to-end delay. A jitter buffer helps with the first four at the expense of the last.

Two redundancy mechanisms are provided. Intra-event updates let a receiver reconstruct the event from any update it receives. Repeating the last packet protects the end of the event. The RFC works an example: with a 25-30% loss rate and a goal that 99% of end-of-event reports get through, each event completion would need to be reported four times, one more than the basic rule, though it calls this objective probably unrealistically stringent. RFC 2198 redundancy can extend the number of retransmissions at lower cost.

Reducing load during congestion means a longer packetization interval, which also needs a longer playout delay. The RFC shows that for very short events the savings are modest: doubling the interval from 25 ms to 50 ms cuts the aggregate bit rate by about 20% while adding 25 ms of end-to-end delay and a one-time gap of the same amount. Documentation for each new event SHOULD discuss which design choices suit its applications.
sections.eli5: When the network is jammed, notes can get lost, so important ones are sent several times. Sending fewer notes helps a little, but then the beep can be a bit late.

sections.title: DTMF Event Codes
sections.content:
The only events this RFC defines are DTMF tones. Digits 0 to 9 use codes 0 to 9, the star key is code 10, the pound key is code 11 and the letters A to D are codes 12 to 15. All are tone events for which the volume field applies. Digits 0 to 9, the star and pound keys are commonly supported, while A to D are less often seen and typically used in special applications such as military networks.

The RFC notes that a gateway detecting DTMF can relieve the receiving end system of that work and avoids low-bit-rate codecs making tones unintelligible, while an Internet phone can emulate DTMF without generating precise tone pairs. For text telephony under ITU-T V.18 Annex B, a sending gateway is RECOMMENDED to detect tones and pauses of at least 40 ms but send tones of at least 70 ms and pauses of at least 50 ms. Receivers converting DTMF events back to tones SHOULD use the second playout algorithm, because an unintended break in a digit can look like an extra digit.
sections.eli5: Each phone button gets its own number, like a secret code: button 5 is note number 5, and the star key is note number 10.

sections.title: The Tone Payload
sections.content:
The tone payload (media type audio/tone) describes a tone by what it is made of instead of by name. That makes recognition faster, since it does not depend on recognizing durations or pauses. The RFC notes there is no single international standard for dial, ringing, busy and similar tones, but they share traits: they are one tone, two or three tones added, or two tones modulated, and almost all use two frequencies.

The first word holds a 9-bit modulation frequency in Hz (zero if none), a T bit that divides it by three so that values such as 16 2/3 Hz can be expressed, a 6-bit volume and a 16-bit duration. Each following 16-bit group has four reserved bits and a 12-bit frequency in Hz. A frequency of zero means silence, and a packet with no frequencies reports silence. A zero duration is not permitted and such tones SHOULD be ignored.

Unlike telephone events, each tone packet stands alone, and its timestamp MUST advance: each new packet's timestamp equals the previous timestamp plus its duration. A lost packet leaves a gap, so the sender SHOULD combine new and old tone reports using RFC 2198 redundancy. If congestion is detected through RTCP, the sender SHOULD lengthen the packetization interval for interim tone reports.
sections.eli5: Instead of saying which button was pressed, this way describes the sound itself: which pitches to play, how loud, and for how long.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
These payloads inherit the security considerations of RTP (RFC 3550) and of any RTP profile in use, with further notes in RFC 2198. The telephone-event payload is highly compressed, so a change of just one bit can change the decoded meaning a lot. For that reason message integrity MUST be provided for it.

To protect both confidentiality and integrity, compliant implementations SHOULD implement the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP). The right key distribution method varies by application, and other means giving equivalent protection may be preferable in some deployments. The RFC also observes that, given robust low-overhead tone generation in the gateway, the payload does not create a significant denial-of-service risk from uneven receiver processing cost.
sections.eli5: A tiny note can mean something totally different if one dot flips, so these notes must be protected from tampering, ideally by locking the whole call.

sections.title: The Event Code Registry
sections.content:
Event codes in the audio/telephone-event type are registered with IANA under the Specification Required and Expert Review policies. The expert checks that the meaning of an event is clearly documented, that it cannot be represented by an existing code, and that the number of events is the minimum needed. Each event's documentation MUST say whether it is a state, a tone or another type, and whether the volume field applies.

Legal codes range from 0 to 255, and the initial registry holds the sixteen DTMF events. Codes 23-40, 49 and 52-63 are reserved for events in RFC 4734 (modem, fax and text telephony), and codes 121-137 and 174-205 are reserved for channel-oriented signalling events. Some codes, including 16, are reserved for specifications that revive the matching RFC 2833 events.

The change summary notes that RFC 2833 required every implementation to be able to receive the DTMF events, while this RFC has senders restrict themselves to events the receiver declares. It also says old receivers may be confused by long-event segments and may discard packets with several events. The RFC 2833 events not carried forward are deprecated because they do not appear to have been implemented.
sections.eli5: There is a numbered list of notes, kept by one office. New notes only get a number after an expert checks they are really needed and clearly explained.

viz.caption: PAYLOAD FORMAT FOR NAMED EVENTS (RFC 4733 FIGURE 1)

fields.name: Event
fields.desc: Number from 0 to 255 identifying the event.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: Set when this packet contains the end of the event.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; sender sets zero, receiver ignores.

fields.name: Volume
fields.desc: Power level in dBm0 with sign dropped, 0 to -63.

fields.name: Duration
fields.desc: Duration so far in timestamp units, network byte order.

items.label: A to D
items.desc: Less commonly used digits; volume applies.

data.title: Tone payload: first word and one frequency word

fields.name: Modulation
fields.desc: Modulation frequency in Hz; zero if none.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: If set, the modulation frequency is divided by three.

fields.name: Volume
fields.desc: Power level in dBm0 with the sign dropped.

fields.name: Duration
fields.desc: Tone duration in timestamp units; zero is not permitted.

fields.name: Frequency
fields.desc: A tone frequency in Hz; zero means silence.

fields.name: Frequency
fields.desc: A second frequency, if any; more may follow.
